title: Intravitreal Tamponade Dynamics: Gas vs. Silicone Oil
summary: Mastering the selection of intraocular tamponade agents is critical for success in vitreoretinal surgery. This guide compares the physical properties, clinical applications, and complication profiles of pneumatic (gas) versus liquid (silicone oil) tamponades.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Intravitreal tamponades are agents used in pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) to provide internal support to the retina. They act by surface tension, counteracting vitreous traction and preventing fluid flow through retinal breaks. Gas (SF6, C3F8) provides temporary expansion and absorption, whereas Silicone Oil provides long-term, non-absorbable support.

sections.title: Red Flags: Tamponade Contraindications
content: Nitrous Oxide (N2O) use: Rapidly expands intraocular gas, causing catastrophic IOP spike.
Air Travel: Forbidden with gas until resorption (risk of severe ocular hypertension).
Silicone Oil in Pseudophakes: Increased risk of oil emulsification and migration into anterior chamber.
High IOP during Oil fill: Risk of Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO).

sections.title: Management Process: The Surgical Path
content: Step 1: Perform complete vitrectomy and fluid-air exchange.
Step 2: Isolate retinal breaks and perform laser retinopexy.
Step 3: Calculate gas concentration based on altitude (e.g., higher altitude = higher concentration).
Step 4: For Oil: Use 1000cs for ease of injection/removal vs 5000cs for long-term stabilization.
Step 5: Post-operative monitoring of IOP and corneal endothelial health.

content.explanation: SF6 lasts for 6 (weeks/2), C3F8 lasts for 8 (weeks). Remember: C3F8 is 'Eight' (F-eight).

sections.title: Complication Profiles
content: Gas: Cataract progression, IOP spikes, retinal re-detachment if gas bubble undersized.
Silicone Oil: Emulsification (oil droplets in AC), Glaucoma (pupillary block/peripheral anterior synechiae), Band keratopathy, Hyphema.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always check IOP in the first 6 hours post-op for gas patients; the expansion phase is critical.
Silicone oil requires surgical removal; leaving it in too long can lead to secondary 'oil-induced' glaucoma.
Use 5000cs silicone oil for patients with complex PVR to minimize the rate of emulsification compared to 1000cs.
Topical glaucoma medications (e.g., Timolol) are often prophylactic in the immediate post-oil period.
